text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Safety note: An intermittent crank-no-start in rain can leave you stranded in traffic or at intersections, but your data does not indicate an immediate brake, steering, fuel leak, or airbag hazard.
- Root cause with confidence percentage: Most likely intermittent moisture-related ignition or engine-position signal loss during cranking, with the strongest suspects being a degraded ignition coil/coil boot area, crankshaft position sensor signal dropout, or water intrusion at engine electrical connectors/grounds; confidence 68%.
- No OBD-II diagnostic trouble codes were provided or auto-detected, so no code-specific set conditions can be tied to the fault. That matters because a true charging-system failure, immobilizer fault, or many hard sensor failures on a 2009 Honda Civic often do set codes or warning lamps; your “no warning lamps” and “runs fine once started” pattern pushes the diagnosis toward an intermittent input that fails only during wet cranking conditions.
- Component failure analysis: Rain raises surface conductivity and lowers insulation resistance. On an aging Civic, moisture can bridge tiny cracks in coil housings, boots, plug well seals, CKP/CMP connector seals, or ground eyelets. During cranking, battery voltage is already depressed by starter load; if a sensor or ignition component is marginal, the lower cranking voltage plus moisture leakage can collapse spark energy or corrupt the crank signal enough that the PCM withholds fuel/spark synchronization. Once the engine starts and alternator output raises system voltage, the same weak component may behave normally.
- Alternator relevance: An “inconclusive” alternator bench or in-car test does not fit the symptom as cleanly as ignition/sensor moisture sensitivity. A weak alternator causes low state of charge after repeated trips, dim lamps, battery warning behavior, and often slow crank rather than a normal-speed crank-no-start that is weather-linked. It is still worth verifying charging voltage because low reserve voltage can amplify the real fault.
- Age considerations for this specific equipment: A 2009 Civic is old enough that rubber seals, connector weather-packs, coil epoxy, and engine grounds commonly age out even if mileage is unknown. Unknown mileage lowers confidence because high-mileage Civics also see fuel pump wear and relay/contact degradation, but the rain correlation remains the strongest clue.
- Data Needed
- Cranking RPM on a scan tool during a no-start event, with pass threshold above about 150 rpm and stable.
- Spark test result during the wet no-start, using an adjustable spark tester set to 25–30 kV.
- Fuel pressure during the wet no-start, with key-on and cranking readings in psi.
- Charging voltage at idle with accessories on, in volts, plus AC ripple in mV.
- Photos or notes of any water intrusion around cowl, coil cover area, under-hood fuse box, and engine grounds.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- 1) Moisture-sensitive ignition secondary leak or weak coil/boot assembly: Most likely because the failure is random in rain, the engine runs fine once started, and there are no warning lamps. Wet insulation leakage is classic for intermittent no-start or rough start without stored codes.
- 2) Crankshaft position sensor or CKP connector moisture/voltage dropout: Strong alternative because the PCM must see a valid crank signal to time spark and injector pulse. A missing CKP during cranking can produce a clean crank-no-start with no immediate lamp complaint if the dropout is brief or not captured.
- 3) Main relay/fuel pump power delivery issue aggravated by humidity: Common Honda pattern historically, though more famous on older Civics/Accords. It fits random no-starts, but rain as the trigger is less classic than heat soak. It is ruled in if spark is present but fuel pressure or injector pulse is absent during the event.
- 4) Low cranking voltage from charging deficiency or parasitic discharge: Possible because a marginal electrical system gets worse in wet weather, but ruled down because you already replaced battery and starter and did not report slow crank, dimming, or battery lamp behavior.
- 5) Immobilizer/key recognition issue: Less likely because Honda immobilizer problems usually flash the green key indicator and are not weather-specific. It can mimic crank-no-start, but your “runs fine once started” and rain link argue against it.
- 6) Flooding from coolant temp sensor bias or intake air sensor issue: Possible but lower likelihood because these usually create repeatable cold-start issues and often set codes or fuel-trim symptoms once running.
- 7) Fuel pump wear: Always possible on an older Civic, especially if mileage is high, but fuel pumps are not usually selectively rain-sensitive unless there is connector or relay moisture intrusion.
- Alternatives that can produce the same no-code crank-no-start pattern and are commonly misdiagnosed: CKP sensor dropout, ignition coil leakage, main relay failure, and low cranking voltage can all produce no-start with no stored code if the event is brief or the PCM never achieves stable synchronization.
- Equipment-specific failure patterns for 2009 Civic: Aging coil boots and spark plug tube seals, corroded grounds, under-hood fuse/relay box moisture issues, CKP/CMP connector degradation, and occasional charging-system weakness under load are all real-world patterns on this platform.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- 1) Battery and cranking voltage drop test; tool required: DVOM with min/max capture. Procedure: Measure battery open-circuit voltage after sitting, then voltage at the battery during cranking and voltage drop from battery negative to engine block while cranking. Expected reading: 12.4–12.7 V rested, not below 9.6 V during 15-second crank at about 70°F, and ground-side drop under 0.2 V. Fail threshold: below 9.6 V cranking or over 0.2 V ground drop indicates electrical support problem. Fair shop cost: $0–$45 if bundled into diagnosis, basis 0.2–0.3 book hr × $120–$150/hr prevailing labor rate.
- 2) Charging system output and ripple test; tool required: DVOM and preferably scope. Procedure: Measure charging voltage at idle and 2,000 rpm with blower/headlamps on, then AC ripple across battery. Expected reading: 13.5–14.8 V charging and AC ripple generally under 100 mV on a healthy alternator. Fail threshold: below 13.2 V loaded, above 15.0 V, or ripple over about 300 mV suggests alternator/diode issue. Fair shop cost: $25–$60, basis 0.2–0.4 book hr × $120–$150/hr.
- 3) Scan-tool cranking data capture during failure; tool required: enhanced scan tool with live data. Procedure: During a no-start, watch engine RPM, ECT, IAT, immobilizer status if available, and pending codes. Expected reading: stable cranking RPM above about 150 rpm and plausible temperature values near ambient/coolant reality. Fail threshold: 0 rpm while cranking points strongly to CKP signal loss; implausible temp values indicate fueling bias. Fair shop cost: $60–$120, basis 0.5–0.8 book hr × $120–$150/hr.
- 4) Spark output test during no-start; tool required: adjustable spark tester. Procedure: Disconnect one coil output path safely and verify spark can jump a 25–30 kV gap during cranking. Expected reading: strong blue spark consistently jumping 25–30 kV. Fail threshold: weak/intermittent/no spark indicates ignition primary/secondary or sync issue. Fair shop cost: $60–$105, basis 0.5–0.7 book hr × $120–$150/hr.
- 5) Fuel pressure test during no-start; tool required: fuel pressure gauge with Honda-compatible adapter. Procedure: Measure key-on and cranking pressure. Expected reading: approximately 50–57 psi on many Civic returnless systems, but the shop must verify exact engine spec by VIN/engine code. Fail threshold: pressure materially below spec during crank or rapid bleed-down with no start. Fair shop cost: $90–$150, basis 0.7–1.0 book hr × $120–$150/hr.
- 6) Injector pulse/noid light test; tool required: noid light or lab scope. Procedure: Check for injector command during the no-start. Expected reading: rhythmic pulse while cranking. Fail threshold: no pulse with no spark and 0 rpm points to CKP/sync issue; no pulse with spark may indicate immobilizer/PCM logic issue. Fair shop cost: $45–$90, basis 0.3–0.6 book hr × $120–$150/hr.
- 7) Coil boot, plug well, and connector moisture inspection; tool required: borescope/inspection light and spray bottle if reproducing carefully. Procedure: Inspect for water tracks, oil in plug wells, cracked boots, green corrosion, and loose seals; if needed, lightly mist suspect areas while monitoring misfire/no-start behavior. Expected reading: dry wells, intact boots, no carbon tracking. Fail threshold: visible tracking, moisture intrusion, or immediate symptom reproduction. Fair shop cost: $60–$120, basis 0.5–0.8 book hr × $120–$150/hr.
- 8) CKP waveform integrity test; tool required: lab scope. Procedure: Backprobe CKP sensor and compare waveform amplitude and continuity during cranking dry versus wet conditions. Expected reading: clean repeating waveform with no dropouts; exact amplitude depends on sensor type and cranking speed, but the key pass criterion is stable pattern without missing segments. Fail threshold: dropout, distortion, or loss of signal during no-start. Fair shop cost: $120–$225, basis 1.0–1.5 book hr × $120–$150/hr.
- Total diagnostic budget line: Fair total for a disciplined diagnosis is $180–$420, basis roughly 1.5–3.0 labor hr × $120–$150/hr prevailing labor rate, depending on whether the fault can be reproduced wet.
- The ONE test that must be completed and shown to the customer BEFORE any part is purchased: A captured no-start event proving which of the three is missing during cranking—RPM signal, spark, or fuel pressure. If they cannot show that, they are guessing.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Question 1: “During the no-start, what cranking RPM did the PCM report, and can you show me the scan capture?” Competent answer: “It showed 0 rpm or unstable rpm during the failure, here is the saved data/PID screenshot.” Red-flag answer: “We don’t need scan data; these cars just need an alternator/sensor.”
- Question 2: “What was battery voltage during cranking and the voltage drop from battery negative to engine block?” Competent answer: “Cranking stayed above 9.6 V and ground drop was under 0.2 V, or here is the exact fail reading.” Red-flag answer: “Battery is new so voltage is fine.”
- Question 3: “Did you verify spark with an adjustable tester during the no-start, and what kV gap did it jump?” Competent answer: “Yes, it did or did not jump 25–30 kV consistently; here is the result.” Red-flag answer: “We pulled a plug and eyeballed spark.”
- Question 4: “What was fuel pressure during the no-start, and what exact Honda spec did you compare it to?” Competent answer: “Pressure was X psi versus spec Y psi from service info; here is the gauge photo.” Red-flag answer: “Fuel pump sounds okay.”
- Question 5: “If you suspect the alternator, what loaded charging voltage and AC ripple did you measure?” Competent answer: “Loaded output was X volts and ripple was Y mV; here is the printout.” Red-flag answer: “The tester said inconclusive, so we recommend replacing it.”
- Specific artifacts they must physically show you: scan report printout or screenshot with live cranking data, recorded voltage-drop readings, fuel-pressure gauge photo or worksheet, and the old replaced part if any part is sold to you.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: “I’ve done some research and want to understand how you proved the cause, especially since it happens randomly in rain.”
- Phrasing: Use curiosity language like “Can you walk me through the readings you got?” instead of “How do I know you’re not guessing?”
- Example dialogue: “I’ve done some research and want to understand—during the no-start, did the PCM show cranking RPM, and can you show me that capture?”
- Example dialogue: “I’ve done some research and want to understand—what was the charging voltage under load and the AC ripple before recommending an alternator?”
- Example dialogue: “I’ve done some research and want to understand—did you confirm whether spark or fuel pressure was missing during the actual failure?”
- Response handling: If they get defensive, say “I’m not questioning your experience; I just want the measurements that justify the repair.”
- Exit strategy: “Thanks for your time. I’m going to hold off until I have the test results documented.”
- NEVER say: “My AI report says...” or “I got a second opinion online.”
- ALWAYS say: “I’ve done some research and want to understand...”

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Most likely repair path is diagnosis first, then one targeted repair based on proof. Because no code and no confirmed failed part exist yet, any full repair quote before testing is premature.
- Diagnostic fee norms: Fair diagnosis is $180–$420, basis 1.5–3.0 labor hr × $120–$150/hr prevailing labor rate. A fair shop often credits some or all of that toward the repair if you authorize the fix the same visit.
- If the fault proves to be one ignition coil on a 2009 Civic: OEM/Denso/Hitachi-quality coil typically $60–$140 each published part price range from mainstream online parts retailers/dealer-counter equivalents; labor typically 0.3–0.6 book hr × $120–$150/hr = $36–$90; fair installed total for one coil is $96–$230 plus any diagnostic fee.
- If the fault proves to be a full set of four coil boots or four coils due to visible cracking/tracking: quality aftermarket boots/coils can range $80–$320 total published part price range depending on brand; labor 0.5–1.0 book hr × $120–$150/hr = $60–$150; fair installed total is $140–$470 plus diagnostic fee. Replacing all four without proof is not automatically justified.
- If the fault proves to be spark plugs and tube seal moisture contamination: NGK plugs typically $25–$60 per set published part price range; valve cover tube seal/gasket set typically $25–$70 published part price range; labor 1.0–2.0 book hr × $120–$150/hr = $120–$300; fair installed total is $170–$430 plus diagnostic fee.
- If the fault proves to be crankshaft position sensor: quality sensor typically $40–$120 published part price range; labor commonly 0.8–1.5 book hr × $120–$150/hr = $96–$225 depending on engine/access; fair installed total is $136–$345 plus diagnostic fee.
- If the fault proves to be alternator: quality aftermarket or reman alternator typically $180–$380 published part price range, OEM often higher; labor commonly 1.2–2.0 book hr × $120–$150/hr = $144–$300; fair installed total is $324–$680 plus diagnostic fee.
- Labor padding warning: If a shop charges more than about 30% above the applicable book time without a documented access issue, that is padded labor.
- Fair total price range: Because the failed part is not yet proven, the fair all-in path is diagnosis $180–$420 plus one targeted repair typically landing between $96–$680 depending on what testing proves.
- OVERCHARGE LINE: For the most expensive plausible common repair here—alternator replacement plus full fair diagnosis—the excessive threshold starts above $1,100, basis upper fair diagnosis $420 + upper fair alternator repair $680 = $1,100. Above that, the quote is excessive unless they document unusual corrosion, seized hardware, or additional confirmed faults.
- No shop quote was provided, so no FAIR/HIGH/RIPOFF verdict can be rendered yet.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Exact parts-cannon sequence shops run for this failure: battery, then starter, then alternator, then fuel pump, then crank sensor, then all four coils. Each is a guess unless they first prove what is missing during the actual no-start.
- Why battery is often a guess here: You already have a new battery, and a battery issue usually causes slow crank or low-voltage symptoms, not a rain-linked normal-speed crank-no-start.
- Why starter is often a guess here: A starter causes no-crank or weak-crank, not “cranks but won’t start.”
- Why alternator is often a guess here: Alternators charge after the engine starts; they do not directly create a one-off wet crank-no-start unless low system reserve is documented with voltage/ripple testing.
- Why fuel pump is often a guess here: Without a fuel-pressure reading during failure, replacing a pump is blind.
- Why crank sensor is often a guess here: It is a valid suspect, but only a scan RPM loss or scope dropout proves it.
- Why all four coils are often a guess here: Moisture can affect one coil boot or one plug well; replacing all four without visible tracking or failed spark testing is upselling.
- Dollar thresholds specific to this repair: Diagnosis-only above $420 is padded unless they spent more than 3.0 documented hours reproducing the wet fault; a single-target repair path above $1,100 all-in is excessive based on upper fair diagnosis $420 plus upper fair alternator repair $680.
- Walk away NOW triggers: refusal to show cranking RPM or fuel-pressure data, “we replace alternator and battery as a set,” “the tester was inconclusive so we’ll start with the alternator,” diagnostic fee with no recorded readings, or recommending multiple ignition/fuel parts before proving spark versus fuel loss.
- Line items to refuse outright for this job: “Preventive fuel pump replacement” — “Please don’t replace a fuel pump without a pressure reading during the failure.”
- Line items to refuse outright for this job: “Alternator because test was inconclusive” — “Please verify loaded voltage and AC ripple first.”
- Line items to refuse outright for this job: “All coils as a set” — “Please identify the failed cylinder/coil or show visible tracking and failed spark output first.”

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: Up to $180–$420 for diagnosis only, tied to 1.5–3.0 labor hr × $120–$150/hr prevailing labor rate, provided they document cranking RPM, spark/fuel status, and charging readings.
- Reject outright: Any parts replacement before they capture the no-start and prove whether RPM signal, spark, or fuel pressure is missing.
- Get a second opinion when: The first shop cannot reproduce the fault, cannot provide readings, or jumps straight to alternator/fuel pump/coil replacement.
- What the second shop must be told: “Intermittent crank-no-start, seems rain-related, battery and starter are new, no warning lamps, no codes detected.”
- What NOT to tell the second shop: Do not suggest the alternator, fuel pump, or crank sensor by name; let them diagnose from symptoms and measurements.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation explanation: Your Civic needs four things to start: adequate cranking speed, valid crank/cam synchronization, strong spark, and correct fuel pressure/injector pulse. The PCM watches crankshaft position to know engine speed and position; if that signal is missing or corrupted, it cannot time spark and fuel correctly. The ignition coils must transform battery voltage into tens of thousands of volts to jump the spark plug gap. The fuel system must maintain pressure while the injectors pulse fuel into the cylinders.
- Why rain matters physically: Water is not a perfect conductor, but dirty water on aged insulation becomes conductive enough to leak high voltage. A cracked coil boot or carbon-tracked plug well can let spark energy bleed to ground instead of jumping the plug gap. Moisture can also wick into connectors, changing resistance and distorting low-voltage sensor signals like CKP. During cranking, system voltage is lower than when running, so marginal components fail first at start-up.
- Why it runs fine once started: Once the engine catches, alternator output raises system voltage and ignition energy reserve. Heat can also dry a marginal connector or boot enough that the symptom disappears until the next wet event.
- Why no warning lamps does not clear the car: Many intermittent start failures happen too briefly to mature a code, or the PCM never gets enough stable runtime during the failed event to store useful data.
- Prevention tips specific to this equipment: Keep the cowl drains clear so water does not overflow toward harnesses and the under-hood fuse box; inspect coil boots and plug wells for oil or water at tune-up time; keep battery terminals and engine grounds clean and tight; avoid engine-bay pressure washing on an older Civic.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Specific part numbers when possible: Exact part numbers depend on engine variant and VIN, so the shop should confirm by VIN before ordering. For spark plugs, NGK is commonly the OE supplier family for Honda applications; for coils and sensors, Denso/Hitachi/NTK are generally safer than no-name economy brands.
- Why OEM is or is not critical: For crank sensors and charging components, OEM or top-tier OE-supplier quality matters because signal integrity and regulator calibration are important. For ignition coils, high-quality aftermarket from an OE supplier can be acceptable; ultra-cheap marketplace coils are false economy on Hondas.
- Pricing sources and alternatives: Dealer/OEM parts usually run higher than RockAuto or major online retailers by roughly 20–80% depending on component. That premium can be worth it for CKP sensors and some alternators; it is less critical for spark plugs and sometimes coils if the brand is truly OE-equivalent.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor on the numbers: “I’m comfortable authorizing diagnosis in the fair range of $180–$420, based on 1.5–3.0 hours at about $120–$150 an hour, but I need the no-start readings before any parts are purchased.”
- Labor justification question: “What labor guide are you using—Alldata, Mitchell, or Motor—and what book time does it show for this exact repair?”
- If they quote an alternator: “My understanding is the fair installed range is about $324–$680 plus diagnosis, based on 1.2–2.0 hours at $120–$150/hr and a published part price range of about $180–$380. Can you show me the loaded voltage and ripple that justify it?”
- Walk-away point in dollars: If the all-in quote exceeds $1,100 before they document unusual access problems or multiple confirmed faults, thank them and leave. That number is consistent with upper fair diagnosis $420 plus upper fair alternator repair $680.
- Leverage plays specific to this case: Because the fault is weather-related, ask to leave the car overnight or during rain so they can reproduce it; authorize diagnosis only, not repair; decline bundled “starting/charging package” add-ons; if they insist on parts first, use that as your cue to get a second opinion.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: Moisture-sensitive ignition secondary leak or coil/boot/plug-well issue, 68% confidence, because rain correlation is strong, no warning lamps are reported, and the engine runs normally once started.
- Secondary cause: Crankshaft position sensor or connector signal dropout during wet cranking, 22% confidence, because a lost RPM signal can create a clean crank-no-start with no immediate code and then behave normally once dry or once voltage rises.
- Tertiary cause: Fuel pump/main relay power delivery issue, 10% confidence, because it can mimic the symptom but is less specifically tied to rain than ignition leakage or connector moisture on this platform.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate actions required: Get a shop to capture the failure and prove whether RPM signal, spark, or fuel pressure is missing before authorizing any part.
- Future maintenance schedule: At the next tune-up or inspection, have the shop inspect spark plug wells, coil boots, cowl drains, battery terminals, and engine grounds; if plugs are overdue by maintenance schedule or age, replace with correct NGK/Denso specification.
- Warning signs to monitor: Note whether the engine cranks at normal speed, whether the green key immobilizer lamp flashes, whether tach/RPM shows movement during crank, whether the problem follows heavy rain or car washes, and whether any rough running occurs for the first 30 seconds after a wet start.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Honda/Acura service information portal for VIN-specific procedures and specs, including charging-system, CKP, and fuel-pressure test procedures: https://techinfo.honda.com
- NHTSA 2009 Honda Civic complaints and manufacturer communications, useful for checking any starting/charging-related bulletins or patterns tied to your exact model: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle/2009/HONDA/CIVIC
- Civic owner and technician pattern database with symptom-specific threads on wet-weather no-start, coil boot tracking, relay issues, and CKP faults; use for pattern recognition only, not as sole proof: https://www.civicforums.com/forums/ and https://www.8thcivic.com/forums/
- Applicable technical guidance note: Because no VIN, engine submodel, or confirmed DTC is provided, I cannot responsibly name a single exact Honda TSB as definitive for your car without risking mismatch. The shop should verify by VIN in Honda service information and show you the bulletin number if they claim one applies.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize diagnosis only, capped at $180–$420 based on 1.5–3.0 labor hr × $120–$150/hr, and require proof of what is missing during the actual no-start: RPM signal, spark, or fuel pressure.
- Do not approve an alternator, fuel pump, crank sensor, or full coil set unless the shop shows the specific failed reading and the test result that confirms it.
- If the first shop cannot provide cranking RPM, spark test, fuel-pressure reading, and charging/ripple numbers, get a second opinion and describe only the symptoms: “2009 Civic, intermittent rain-related crank-no-start, battery and starter new, no warning lamps.”
